fixes.explanation: Useless is a harsh word, and Paul doesn't use it. He says that when he does what he doesn't want to do, “…I admit that the law is good.” He keeps agreeing with the law while he's in the middle of his struggle. That's some humility right there.

That's it. Paul says, “…it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.” He names sin as the one at work inside him. And the same line shows up again in verse 20, so you can spot it twice in this passage.

Pride is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word on the page. Paul says, “…it is sin living in me that does it.” Pride is a sneaky one, I'll give you that, but it isn't named in these verses. The word Paul picks is sin, and he says it's living in him.

Fear doesn't show up in this verse, baker. Paul says, “…it is sin living in me that does it.” That's the word he picks, and the same line comes back in verse 20. Remember that word, because it keeps returning through the passage.

Boasting isn't the word here, friend. Paul calls himself unspiritual and sold as a slave to sin just a few verses back (Romans 7:14). What he says is, “For in my inner being I delight in God’s law.” Delight is the word, not boasting.

Paul is writing to people in Rome who are loved by God (Romans 1:7), so I see why Rome came to mind. But this war isn't with any government. He says the other law is “…warring against the law of my mind…” The fight is happening inside him.

That's his question. Paul cries, “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” He doesn't ask who will help him try harder. He asks who will rescue him. Rescue is the word he picks.
Yes! Paul writes, “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Notice where it lands, right after his cry for a rescuer. He points straight to God and to Jesus.

Gamaliel was a teacher of the law, honored by all the people (Acts 5:34), and Paul tells us he was educated under him (Acts 22:3). But Paul doesn't thank him in this verse, friend. When he cries out for a rescuer, his thanks goes elsewhere: “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!”
